recent_posts.title: Why pricing should be treated like a product not a policy
recent_posts.summary: Elena Verna shares key lessons from her Stripe Sessions talk on treating pricing and packaging as a product rather than a fixed policy. Drawing from her experience at Lovable, she argues companies underinvest in monetization as a growth lever. Key takeaways include: normalizing pricing iteration (Lovable changed pricing 10+ times in a year without customer revolt), treating freemium as a strategic investment rather than a cost center, ungating AI features to let customers experience value before paying, and moving beyond subscription-only models to hybrid approaches like top-ups. She recommends getting billing infrastructure right, assigning clear monetization ownership, and running pricing changes like experiments rather than multi-year transformation projects.

recent_posts.title: How product marketing works at AI-native speed
recent_posts.summary: A guest post from Lovable's Core PMM describing how product marketing has evolved at AI-native speed. Key practices include tiered launch systems that let engineers and PMs self-serve launches without PMM bottlenecks, data-driven ICP reviews done weekly rather than annually, continuous customer interviews with standardized questions to capture real language and pain points, and a simplified messaging framework accessible to the whole org. A bonus section advocates for AI agents that let anyone query messaging, ICP data, and launch info in natural language rather than hunting through stale docs.

recent_posts.title: What happens to your product when AI agents become the primary users
recent_posts.summary: As AI agents increasingly interact with software on behalf of humans via protocols like MCP (Model Context Protocol), the traditional concept of an ICP (human user) is being disrupted. Products that relied on UI polish, onboarding flows, and user habituation for stickiness may find those moats evaporate — agents evaluate purely on output quality, reliability, and structured accessibility. Companies need to expose their products via MCP or equivalent interfaces, prioritize clean documentation and predictable outputs over UI, and rethink distribution as 'making it easy for agents to find you' rather than funneling humans through conversion flows. The market will likely split: some products become invisible infrastructure powering agent workflows, while others double down on genuinely lovable human experiences. Most B2B software will fall into the former category.

recent_posts.title: A millennial in tech reflects on AI disrupting careers and expertise
recent_posts.summary: A personal reflection on navigating the AI-driven shift in tech from a millennial's perspective. Explores feelings of being perpetually behind, the erosion of hard-won expertise as AI flattens skill hierarchies, the social pressure of fake confidence online, and the uncomfortable economic questions around compensation and knowledge work. Argues that value is shifting away from execution toward taste, judgment, and prioritization — skills that are harder to build and teach.

recent_posts.title: Five retention techniques recently tested at Lovable and what they yielded
recent_posts.summary: Five recently tested retention techniques for subscription products: adding a hidden 'lite' plan in the cancellation flow, in-app payment failure notifications (which improved recovery rate by 50%), daily free credit grants to maintain engagement, credit rollover policies to reduce resentment from unused credits, and ad hoc top-up payments. Also covers two key laws of retention testing: results take months to observe, and effective retention tactics often feel counterintuitive because they require giving value away short-term to improve long-term monetization.

recent_posts.title: Why making revenue your north star metric will kill your company
recent_posts.summary: Revenue addiction — optimizing everything for short-term revenue at the expense of innovation, culture, and customer value — has always been a slow killer for companies. In the current AI disruption era, it has become fatal. Companies fixated on quarterly revenue targets kill risk-taking, suppress long-term bets, poison culture, and lose sight of customers. The alternative is treating revenue as an output of delivering customer value, not the primary objective. Using Lovable as an example, the author advocates for North Star metrics tied to product engagement and qualitative customer satisfaction scores. Revenue addiction is nearly impossible to cure from within; employees should plan their exit if they see the signs, while founders and execs must make structural changes at the leadership level before it's too late.

recent_posts.title: The Minimum Lovable Product Era
recent_posts.summary: The MVP (Minimum Viable Product) concept has been degraded into shipping bare-minimum functional products, which made sense when dev costs were high. Now that AI has collapsed software development costs and commoditized basic functionality, the new baseline should be MLP: Minimum Lovable Product. An MLP is the earliest version that creates genuine emotional connection with users through personality, delight moments, and human touches. Lovability is argued to be the last defensible moat since AI can replicate features but not the emotional relationship users build with a product. Practical advice includes starting with a specific customer segment, building 'lovemarks' into the roadmap as deliberate priorities, using AI to accelerate lovable interactions, and always asking 'is this lovable?' before shipping.

recent_posts.title: Why becoming AI-native now is the biggest career opportunity in years
recent_posts.summary: A call-to-action essay arguing that the window to gain a career advantage by becoming AI-native is measured in months, not years. Using a personal anecdote of shipping a production code fix via Cursor and Claude Code without an engineering background, the author contends that AI is collapsing the gap between intent and execution. Five concrete steps are recommended: vibe-code a version of your company's product, make AI your default for all work, retry AI tasks weekly as capabilities improve rapidly, start a side project, and find an AI-native mentor. The core argument is that the biggest career risk isn't AI replacing jobs—it's complacency while early adopters compound their advantage.

recent_posts.title: How adding credit top-ups improved engagement and retention at Lovable
recent_posts.summary: Lovable, an AI product, shifted from subscription-only billing to include credit top-ups after user complaints and irregular usage patterns. Through A/B testing, they found a 20% premium on top-ups (vs. subscriptions) increased engagement, improved paid retention by 7%, and generated 20%+ of bookings within a week—without cannibalizing subscription revenue. The change aligned monetization with actual user behavior, proving that optimizing solely for ARR can harm long-term engagement and retention.

recent_posts.title: How AI vibecoding enables satellite apps to replace lead magnets
recent_posts.summary: AI-powered 'vibecoding' tools are transforming engineering-as-marketing by enabling non-technical teams to rapidly build 'Satellite Apps'—lightweight, free micro-products that demonstrate value throughout the customer journey. These interactive experiences replace traditional lead magnets like gated PDFs, allowing companies to show rather than tell product value. The approach unlocks product-led growth tactics for sales-led organizations and enables PLG companies to create value-proving experiences across their entire funnel, from acquisition through activation.
